epigrafe.descrizione: A handle from a Roman Amphora. The rest of the vessel is missing. The large handle is constructed from a sandy fabric. There is a stamp along the central ridge of the upper handle, but this is illegible. The handle's size, robustity, and broadly sweeping curve are indicative of it being Dressel type 20, which would date it to between AD 50 and 250, though this may be from the late series.…

epigrafe.descrizione: A Roman silver denarius of Mark Anthony, dating to c.32-31BC. Travelling mint. Obverse: Galley with banners. Inscription: ANT AVG III VIR RPC. Reverse: Aquila between two standards. Inscription: illegible. Crawford, pp. 539-541, No. 544. These coins were struck by Mark Antony for the use of his fleet and legions when he was preparing for the struggle with Octavius, which culminated in the Battle of Actium on the 2nd of September, 31 BC (Grueber, 1970, 526)

epigrafe.descrizione: A lead spindle whorl of Walton Rogers form A1, probably dating from the Early Medieval period, about AD 500 - 850. The whorl is circular and has one flat face and one convex face, a shape which is classified as form A1, thought to be in use in AD 500 - 1000. It has a circular central aperture of 8mm diameter. This size of spindle hole can suggest an Early to Middle Saxon date. There are three Xs…

Four of the sesterti are fused in two sets of two. The emperors and empresses featured are: Lucius Verus (1); Lucilla (3), Marcus Aurelias (2), Faustina II (2), Lucilla or Faustina (2), Commodus (3), Didius Julianus (1), Septimius Severus (1) and Severus Alexander…

epigrafe.provenienza: contea di ritrovamento: Calderdale (Inghilterra e Galles)
epigrafe.descrizione: A lead discoidal artefact, possibly a cast copy of a Roman nummus dating from AD 364 - 410. It is 14mm in diameter and 4mm thick. It weighs 5.29g. One face is flat and the other is slightly convex. Both are exceedingly worn. If it is a copy of a Roman coin, it is possibly imitating a nummus of the House of Valentinian, dating from AD 364-375, Gloria Romanorum reverse type (Reece Period 19). There is a possible bust right on the obverse, the rounder face. The reverse possible shows the Emperor with standard dragging a captive right with the letters RO visible from the inscription 'GLORIA ROMANORVM'. Mint mark not visible
epigrafe.fotografo: West Yorkshire Archaeology Advisory Service, Ian Whitehead
epigrafe.licenza_metadati: CC BY-SA 4.0 (schede del PAS su Wikimedia Commons)

epigrafe.descrizione: CORONER'S REPORT. Description of find. A damaged and distorted Roman silver finger-ring with very slender plain tapered hoop, narrow plain shoulders and a tiny flattened oval bezel, now dished through damage. The uneven surface of the bezel (not the remains of an inscription) may be the remains of degraded solder for a (now missing) appliqué. Date: probably 1 st -2 nd century AD. Dimensions: maximum length 23.6 mm. bezel width 5.3 mm. Weight: 2.4 g

epigrafe.descrizione: An incomplete copper alloy dragonesque brooch, dating to the early Roman period (c.AD50-200). The object comprises an incomplete curvilinear plate in an S-shape, with squared bar terminals (one of which is missing). Across the wider body section are two further bars with an inscription between, of which "...N OR..." can be read. The reverse of the object is undecorated. Dimension: Length 29.89mm; Width 23.88mm; Thickness 4.94mm; Weight 7.8gm. The brooch conforms to the type desinated by Hunter (2010) as as Type C3 , S-shaped brooch with bar terminals, and by Mackreth (2011) as DRAG Type 1.a . (see Mackreth 2011, vol1 p186; vol2 Plate 128 no. 7750). Mackreth (2011, vol1 p186) notes the…

epigrafe.descrizione: Cast copper-alloy Roman eagle mount. It is small, quite worn and was not too well made to begin with. The eagle is standing upright, wings stretched out, looking left. Only its outlines are clear; there are no grooves or mouldings to indicate eyes or feathers. The outline of the eagle tapers towards a flat disc with broken-off sides which indicates that the eagle was a centre-piece of a (probably) circular ornament (see below). The reverse is plain except a tapering spike that is coming out of the centre of the mount - probably for attachment to a leather strap or belt. A similar eagle mount was discovered on the banks of the River Eden in Carlisle ('The Swifts') and is now kept in Tullie…

epigrafe.descrizione: A fragment of a cast copper alloy finger ring.The bezel and shoulders only survive. The bezel is a raised, intaglio-style oval with an incised inscription of three letters, probably L R V. The shoulders are decorated with incised lines. The band is broad and flat. Roger Tomlin suggests the following with regard to the inscription: "Judging by the R, it was cut from right to left. My guess is LRV, not IRV, both because the horizontal stroke below 'I' does not extend to the left at all, so is not intended to be a serif (contrast V), and because this is likeliest to be the initials of the wearer's tria nomina, of which the first could not be I. So my guess is L(ucius) R(...) V(...). I can't…

epigrafe.testo: IMP C CARAVSIVS P F [AVG] ; R/ VIR[TVS AVG]
epigrafe.descrizione: A copper alloy radiate of Carausius dating to the period AD 286 - 293 (Reece Period 14), VIR[TVS AVG] reverse type depicting Mars standing left leaning on shield and holding spear. Unattributed mint or Rouen. It is not possible to confirm the inscription IMP C CARAVSIVS P F [AVG] from the image. This legend is unrecorded in RIC for unattributed coins (RIC V, pt 2, p. 545, cf 1047), but is known for Rouen (RIC V, pt 2, p. 523, cf 700, and examples in Sam Moorhead's corpus). Coin to be compared with other coins in corpus. This coin has been included in Sam Moorhead's corpus for RIC

epigrafe.descrizione: Roman copper alloy spoon, 109mm long, 31mm wide and 14mm thick with a weight of 12.06grams. The object consists of an incomplete spoon bowl which would have had an ovoid form. Its handle is almost complete. The 'neck' joining the two parts consists of an openwork sub rectangular attachment. It emerges from just below the rim of the bowl, running outwards from it for about 10mm. This is decorated with a ring and dot depression next to the bowl, followed by a line of semi-circular stamps. It then turns upwards, c.10mm, where it joins the handle. The line of stamps continues over the end of the handle in a diagonal alignment ending at its upper surface. Below this the decoration forms a bird…

The coin depicts the Emperor going right dragging a captive, GLORIA ROMANORVM, struck circa AD 364-78. Obverse description: Diademed, draped and cuirassed bust right. Obverse inscription: Illegible. Reverse description: The Emperor going right holding a standard and dragging a captive. Reverse inscription: [GLORIA ROMANORVM]. Mint mark: Illegible. Die axis: 12

The pseudo-inscription reads DNΛTTΛN_N_T┤T┌ΛNΛNCC (all Ns reversed). This is not a literate inscription but can most plausibly be derived from a literate inscription of Anastasius (DN ANASTASIVS PP AVG), although…

epigrafe.provenienza: contea di ritrovamento: Lincolnshire (Inghilterra e Galles)
epigrafe.descrizione: Silver Finger Ring. Cast TOT ring with a flat oval bezel standing proud of broad flared shoulders, each with a pair of incised grooves framing the bezel. The inscription was perhaps stamped using a straight rectangular stamp and a crescentic stamp, the latter repeated to form the O of the abbreviated word TOT on the bezel. Below the shoulders the band narrows to a D-section hoop. Abraded, and with the narrower part of the band pitted. Suggested date: Later Roman, 200-300. Internal diameter: 19.4mm, Width (at flared shoulder): 8.2mm, Thickness (at bezel): 3.9mm, Weight: 4.73gms. In view of its age and material the object is to be submitted to the Treasure process, Treasure reference 2014 T54

The obverse is restruck over a Gloria Exercitus reverse of 330-340, though the underlying figurative scene is not entirely clear: there may be a quadruped moving left where standards should be! The reverse incorporates lettering perhaps derived from the earlier obverse, in particular the letters [--]CONSTA[--]N[--]. Opposed cut-outs reduce the flan to a figure-of-eight shape recalling that of a Persian shield. Obverse description: Possibly bust right, with underlying features as noted above: a soldier holding spear with lunate ferrule, facing left, is the clearest element of these.…

epigrafe.descrizione: Gold Roman finger ring with inscribed bezel (c. AD 43 - 200). The finger ring has a rectangular-sectioned hoop which widens from a very narrow point to a flat, rectangular bezel. The bezel appears to have been stamped with a rectangular stamp (the outline of which is faintly visible). Incised onto the bezel within the rectangular outline are three initials: G B R. The letters are of unequal size and uncertain execution. The finger ring has been flattened, probably while in the ground, and this has resulted in some fracturing of the hoop at the point where it has been bent. There are a number of similar inscribed gold and silver finger rings of Roman date recorded on the database. These…

epigrafe.provenienza: contea di ritrovamento: North Yorkshire (Inghilterra e Galles)
epigrafe.descrizione: A cast copper-alloy Aucissa brooch of the early Roman period. The brooch is largely complete, missing only the hinge pin. The hinge for the pin was formed by the rolling of the head back onto itself with a verticle slot for the pin. There is some moulded decoration across the breadth of the head, but no stamp or inscription. The bow has a central ridge decorated with a band containing raised circles down its length. The outer edges of the bow are also raised, creating a grooved effect. Further moulded decoration across the breadth of the base of the bow distinguished the beginning of the foot, otherwise undecorated but ending in a spherical knob. The catchplate is nearly complete
epigrafe.fotografo: Museum of Antiquities of the University and Society of Antiquaries of Newcastle upon Tyne, Robert Collins

epigrafe.provenienza: contea di ritrovamento: Nottinghamshire (Inghilterra e Galles)
epigrafe.descrizione: A silver Roman finger ring, Henig Type VIII, of which only the bezel and shoulders survive. The ring bezel is circular and the shoulders are also circular. The hoop is missing. The shoulders are decorated with an incised 'V' with perimeter facets to either side decorated with radiating incised lines. The bezel bears the inscription 'TO', which is an abbreviation for the Celtic god-name Totatis, one of the principal deities in Gaul. Many of these rings are known from the East Midlands, especially in Lincolnshire where the deity appears to have had a large following. epigrafe.provenienza: contea di ritrovamento: Staffordshire (Inghilterra e Galles)
epigrafe.descrizione: An incomplete silver finger ring of Roman date, probably 3rd Century AD. Around 25% of the finger ring is present, consisting of part of the bezel, a shoulder and the start of the hoop. The bezel was originally rectangular in shape, with a recessed border around the edge. The end part of the inscription is present, consisting of the letters 'MT'. This is probably the end of an dedication to either Mars or Mercury. The hoop was probably keeled. The shoulders have been decorated with seven grooved mouldings, creating a ridged effect. The hoop is 13.8 mm wide and 3.1 mm thick. The finger ring fragment is 16.5 mm long, 13.8 mm wide and 3.1 mm thick. It weighs 2.8 g. The finger ring is a light…

epigrafe.provenienza: contea di ritrovamento: West Berkshire (Inghilterra e Galles)
epigrafe.descrizione: A silver Roman Republic denarius issued by C Antius C.f. Restio, and dating to 47 BC (Reece Period 1). Obverse shows the jugate heads of the Dei Penates and the reverse inscription reads C.ANTIVS C . F; Hercules walking right holding club and trophy, cloak over left arm. Mint of Rome. RRC 455/2a; Syd. 971. The coin has been countermarked, once on the reverse with a 'C' like symbol, while the obverse has two countermarks; at 3 o'clock a 'D' shaped mark on its side, and in the centre an inverted 'V'. If the coin is rotated to 6 o'clock, the countermarks appear as 'AV'

epigrafe.provenienza: contea di ritrovamento: Wirral (Inghilterra e Galles)
epigrafe.descrizione: A possible Roman lead curse tablet (AD 43-AD 410). This rolled strip has been deliberately folded three times. On each side there are deliberate linear grooves. The object has a yellowish patina. Other curse tablets have been recorded on the Portable Antiquities Scheme database. See finds: CAM-9EB3F2 , KENT-35F464, LVPL-85ADA3 , LVPL-DEA234 , NARC1463 , NCL-2ABD75, PAS-713571 and WILT-EE1C84
